tips.title: The unit is the formula
tips.body: **km/h** is kilometres **per** hour, so speed is distance ÷ time. **g/cm³** is grams per cm³, so density is mass ÷ volume. **N/m²** is force ÷ area. Read the slash as a division and you never need to recall the formula.

tips.title: Convert the time before dividing
tips.body: 90 minutes is **1.5 hours**. On a calculator an hour and a half is **1.5, never 1.30** — 1.30 means 1 hour 18 minutes. Worth knowing cold: 15 min = 0.25, 20 min = ⅓, 30 min = 0.5, 45 min = 0.75.

tips.title: Average speed is never the mean of the speeds
tips.body: It is **total distance ÷ total time**. 60 km at 60 km/h then 60 km at 30 km/h averages **40**, not 45, because the slow leg takes twice as long. Questions give equal **distances** precisely so the mean is wrong.

tips.title: Let the unit check your division
tips.body: If the answer should be in hours and you have divided litres by litres per minute, the units will not come out right. Writing the unit beside the answer catches a division done the wrong way round, which is otherwise invisible.

steps.title: What makes a measure compound
steps.body:
A **compound measure** is built from two others, and its **units tell you how**.

- **speed** is measured in **km/h** — kilometres **per** hour — so it is distance **÷** time.
- **density** is in **g/cm³**, so it is mass **÷** volume.
- **pressure** is in **N/m²**, so it is force **÷** area.
- **rate of pay** is in **£/hour**, so it is pay **÷** hours.

The slash in the unit **is** the division. That is the most useful fact in the topic: if you can read the units, you can write the formula without remembering it.

$$\text{speed} = \frac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}} \qquad \text{density} = \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}} \qquad \text{pressure} = \frac{\text{force}}{\text{area}}$$

And each rearranges the same way. From $\text{speed} = \dfrac{d}{t}$ you get $d = \text{speed} \times t$ and $t = \dfrac{d}{\text{speed}}$.

steps.title: Getting the units right first
steps.body:
Most lost marks in this topic are **unit** errors, not arithmetic.

**Time is the usual culprit.** A journey of 90 km taking **90 minutes** is not 1 km/h. Convert the minutes to hours first:

$$90 \text{ minutes} = 1.5 \text{ hours}, \qquad \text{speed} = \frac{90}{1.5} = 60 \text{ km/h}$$

The conversions worth knowing by heart:

- 30 minutes $= 0.5$ h, 15 minutes $= 0.25$ h, 45 minutes $= 0.75$ h
- 20 minutes $= \tfrac{1}{3}$ h, 40 minutes $= \tfrac{2}{3}$ h
- For anything else, **divide the minutes by 60**

A warning about the calculator: **1 hour 30 minutes is 1.5, not 1.30.** Typing 1.30 treats it as 1 hour and 18 minutes.

**Match the unit to the question.** If the answer must be in m/s but the distance is in km and the time in minutes, convert both before dividing, not after.

steps.title: Average speed is not the average of the speeds
steps.body:
This is the trap the topic is built around, and it catches almost everyone the first time.

> A car drives 60 km at 60 km/h, then 60 km at 30 km/h. What is its average speed for the whole journey?

The tempting answer is $\dfrac{60 + 30}{2} = 45$ km/h. It is **wrong**.

**Average speed is always total distance ÷ total time.** Work out each leg's time separately:

- First leg: $\dfrac{60}{60} = 1$ hour
- Second leg: $\dfrac{60}{30} = 2$ hours
- Total: $120$ km in $3$ hours, so $\dfrac{120}{3} = 40$ km/h

The answer is **40**, not 45. It is lower than the mean because the car spends **more time** going slowly — twice as long, in fact, so the slow speed counts double.

A table of distances and times, filled in leg by leg, makes this almost automatic and is worth drawing every time.

steps.title: Unit pricing and best value
steps.body:
**Unit pricing** compares products by working out the cost of **one unit** of each — one litre, one gram, one sheet.

> A 6 litre bottle costs £4.50. A 3 litre bottle costs £2.40. Which is better value?

Work in **pence per litre** to avoid decimals:

- Large: $\dfrac{450}{6} = 75$ p per litre
- Small: $\dfrac{240}{3} = 80$ p per litre

The **large** bottle is better value, at 75p per litre against 80p.

Two things make this reliable.

- **Compare the same unit both ways.** Cost per litre or litres per pound — either works, but be clear which, because for *litres per pound* **more** is better while for *pence per litre* **less** is better.
- **State the conclusion.** *The 6 litre bottle is better value because it costs 75p per litre against 80p* is the answer; two numbers alone are not.

check.solution: Times: 2 hours and 4 hours, so 200 km in 6 hours, giving $\dfrac{200}{6} = 33.3$ km/h to 1 d.p. The mean of the speeds, 37.5, is wrong.

steps.title: Going deeper: density, and reading a rate backwards
steps.body:
**Density explains floating.** Water has a density of $1$ g/cm³. Anything **less** dense floats; anything **more** dense sinks. A wooden block at $0.8$ g/cm³ floats; a metal block at $8$ g/cm³ does not. A question asking *will it float?* is asking you to compare with 1.

That also gives a sense check: a density of $0.008$ or $800$ g/cm³ for an ordinary material is wrong by a factor of a thousand, and usually means a unit was not converted.

**Pressure explains why a drawing pin works.** The same force on a **smaller area** gives a **greater pressure**, because pressure is force ÷ area. The pin's point has a tiny area, so the pressure is enormous — which is why it goes into the wood while your thumb does not.

**Reading a rate backwards.** If a tap fills 60 litres in 4 minutes, the rate is 15 litres per minute. But the question may ask how long to fill 200 litres: that is $\dfrac{200}{15} = 13.3$ minutes. Decide which quantity you are dividing by, and let the **unit of the answer** tell you whether you have it right — minutes, not litres.

**A compound measure of a compound measure.** Population density is people per km², fuel consumption is miles per gallon or litres per 100 km. The same reading-the-units method works: *litres per 100 km* means litres ÷ (distance in hundreds of km), and **lower** is better, while for *miles per gallon* **higher** is better. Getting which direction is better is worth as much as the arithmetic.

**And the trap once more.** Average speed is total distance over total time. It equals the mean of the two speeds only when the **times** are equal, not when the distances are — and questions almost always give equal distances precisely so that the mean is wrong.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- A **compound measure** is built from two others, and the **unit tells you the formula**.
- **speed** $=$ distance ÷ time (km/h); **density** $=$ mass ÷ volume (g/cm³); **pressure** $=$ force ÷ area (N/m²).
- Each rearranges three ways: $d = s \times t$, $t = d \div s$, and so on.
- **Convert the time first.** 90 minutes is $1.5$ hours, not 90 and not 1.30.
- 15 min $= 0.25$, 20 min $= \tfrac{1}{3}$, 30 min $= 0.5$, 45 min $= 0.75$.
- **Average speed is total distance ÷ total time**, never the mean of the speeds.
- 60 km at 60 km/h then 60 km at 30 km/h averages **40** km/h, not 45, because more time is spent going slowly.
- **Unit pricing**: work out the cost of one unit, compare, and **state which is better and why**.
- For *cost per unit*, **lower** is better; for *units per pound*, **higher** is.
- Water has density $1$ g/cm³: less dense **floats**, more dense **sinks**, whatever the size.
- The same force on a **smaller area** gives **greater** pressure.
- Let the **unit of the answer** confirm you divided the right way round.

questions.prompt: A car drives 100 km at 50 km/h and then a further 100 km at 25 km/h. Find the average speed for the whole journey, and explain why it is not 37.5 km/h.
questions.solution: Average speed is always the total distance divided by the total time, so both totals must be found first. For the first leg, the time is one hundred divided by fifty, which is two hours. For the second leg, the time is one hundred divided by twenty five, which is four hours. The total distance is two hundred kilometres and the total time is six hours, so the average speed is two hundred divided by six, which is thirty three point three kilometres per hour to one decimal place. The answer is not thirty seven point five, which is the mean of the two speeds, because the car does not spend equal amounts of time at each speed. It spends two hours at fifty kilometres per hour but four hours at twenty five, so the slower speed applies for twice as long and therefore pulls the average down further than a simple mean would. The mean of the speeds would only be correct if the two times were equal, whereas here it is the two distances that are equal.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Each leg's time.**

$$t_1 = \frac{100}{50} = 2 \text{ hours} \qquad t_2 = \frac{100}{25} = 4 \text{ hours}$$

**Totals.** $200$ km in $6$ hours.

$$\text{average speed} = \frac{200}{6} = \mathbf{33.3} \text{ km/h (1 d.p.)}$$

**Why not 37.5?** That is the **mean of the speeds**, which assumes equal **time** at each. Here the car spends **2 hours** fast and **4 hours** slow — twice as long at the slower speed — so the slow leg counts double and drags the average below the mean.

The mean of the speeds is correct only when the **times** are equal. Questions give equal **distances** precisely so that it is not.

questions.prompt: A 750 ml bottle of juice costs £1.80 and a 2 litre bottle costs £4.40. Determine which is better value, showing your comparison clearly.
questions.solution: To compare the two bottles fairly they must be measured in the same unit, so first convert the volumes. The small bottle is seven hundred and fifty millilitres, which is nought point seven five litres, and the large bottle is two litres. Working in pence avoids decimals, so the small bottle costs one hundred and eighty pence and the large costs four hundred and forty pence. The cost per litre of the small bottle is one hundred and eighty divided by nought point seven five, which is two hundred and forty pence per litre. The cost per litre of the large bottle is four hundred and forty divided by two, which is two hundred and twenty pence per litre. Since two hundred and twenty pence is less than two hundred and forty pence, the two litre bottle is better value, costing twenty pence less for every litre of juice.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Match the units first.** $750$ ml $= 0.75$ litres. Work in **pence** to avoid decimals: 180p and 440p.

**Cost per litre.**

$$\text{small} = \frac{180}{0.75} = 240\text{p per litre}$$
$$\text{large} = \frac{440}{2} = 220\text{p per litre}$$

**Conclusion.** $220 < 240$, so the **2 litre bottle is better value**, by 20p per litre.

Two things earn the marks beyond the arithmetic: **converting to a common unit** before comparing, and **stating the conclusion** rather than leaving two numbers on the page.

examTechnique.body:
Read the unit you are asked for before you start, and convert every quantity to match it. Time is where most marks go.

Write the formula down, then rearrange it if you need to. All three of these rearrange the same way.

For a journey in stages, draw a table with a row per leg and columns for distance, speed and time. Fill in each time, then total the distance and the time columns. That makes average speed automatic.

Never average the speeds.

For best value, work out the cost of one unit for each option, compare, and then **write the sentence** saying which is better and by how much.

Put the unit on your answer. It is the quickest check that you divided the right way round.
examinerErrors: Dividing by minutes when the answer is wanted in km/h.
Typing 1.30 on a calculator for one and a half hours.
Taking the mean of two speeds instead of total distance over total time.
Comparing prices without converting to a common unit first.
Giving two cost-per-unit figures without saying which is better value.
Multiplying where the formula divides, usually by not reading the unit.
Omitting the unit, so a wrong division goes unnoticed.
Assuming a denser object always sinks regardless of the liquid.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer reads the required unit first and converts everything to match before any arithmetic, which is why its time conversions are never wrong. For a multi-stage journey it builds a table and totals the columns, so the average speed falls out rather than being guessed at, and it can say why the mean of the speeds is wrong rather than merely knowing that it is. In a value comparison it converts to a common unit, compares, and commits to a conclusion with the figures attached. And it writes the unit on every answer, using it as the check that the division went the right way round.
